Explorando `net_agent` a fondo: Ejemplos paso a paso de cada funcionalidad\n\nNo basta con ver la tabla de firmas: vamos a explorar **cada una de las funcionalidades** de la lib `net_agent` mediante ejemplos progresivos y ejecutables en Ridgun. Empezaremos por las dos recetas tabulares de uso cotidiano y después recorreremos en detalle todos los escenarios funcionales, transformaciones y casos límite verificados en `src/test/ridgun/test net_agent.ridgun`.\n\n### 32.3.1. Ejemplo 1: Flujo principal en estilo tabular con `net_agent`\n\nObserva cómo en Ridgun los signos `=` y los pasos de transformación con `net_agent` quedan alineados como una tabla limpia, sin variables mutables innecesarias ni efectos laterales ocultos:\n\n```ridgun\nimport socket\nimport net_agent\n\nfn :: fin de linea String Int => Int\n      fin de linea s      i   =\n        | i >= (str len s)        = 0 - 1\n        | (str char at s i) == 10 = i\n        | otherwise               = fin de linea s (i + 1)\n\n-- El estado de cada conexión es cuántas líneas ha enviado.\nfn :: responder Int String => ConnStep Int\n      responder n   entrada =  linea vista n entrada (fin de linea entrada 0)\n\nfn :: linea vista Int String  Int => ConnStep Int\n      linea vista n   entrada fin =\n        | fin < 0   = ConnStep n 0 \"\" False\n        | otherwise = ConnStep (n + 1) (fin + 1) (\"eco \" + (str slice entrada 0 fin) + \"\\n\") False\n\nfn :: primero ((Reactor Int) [Int]) => Reactor Int\n      primero (r, _)                =  r\n\n-- Cada vuelta espera como mucho 100 ms a que pase algo, y después responde a quien tenga una línea completa.\nfn :: servir (Reactor Int) Int     => ReactorStats\n      servir r             vueltas =\n        | vueltas <= 0 = reactor stop r 1000\n        | otherwise    = servir (reactor each (primero (reactor turn r [] 100)) 0 (responder)) (vueltas - 1)\n\nfn :: main => ()\n      main =\n        r = reactor start (sock fd (sys tcp listen \"127.0.0.1\" 0 64)) (reactor defaults)\n        echo (accepted_count (servir r 10))\n```\n\n### 32.3.2. Ejemplo 2: Composición segura y manejo de casos de borde\n\nToda función de la lib `net_agent` está diseñada para componerse con guardas booleanas `|` y con el resto de las 38 libs de `ridgun-libs`:\n\n```ridgun\nimport socket\nimport net_agent\n\n-- Límites estrictos: 100 conexiones, 4 KB de entrada y 1 MB de salida por conexión,\n-- 5 s para el primer mensaje y 60 s de inactividad.\nfn :: limites => ReactorConfig\n      limites =\n        c1 = reactor with max conns (reactor defaults) 100\n        c2 = reactor with input limit c1 4096\n        c3 = reactor with output limit c2 1048576\n        c4 = reactor with first message limit c3 5000\n        reactor with idle limit c4 60000\n\n-- A cada conexión nueva se le encola un saludo y se marca para cerrar cuando se haya enviado.\nfn :: saludar (Reactor Int) [Int]      => Reactor Int\n      saludar r             []         =  r\n      saludar r             (id:resto) =  saludar (reactor close after send (reactor send r id (\"hola \" + (reactor peer r id) + \"\\n\")) id) resto\n\nfn :: tras la vuelta ((Reactor Int) [Int]) => Reactor Int\n      tras la vuelta (r, _)                =  saludar r (reactor arrived r)\n\nfn :: una vuelta (Reactor Int) => Reactor Int\n      una vuelta r             =  tras la vuelta (reactor turn r [] 100)\n\nfn :: main => ()\n      main =\n        r0 = reactor start (sock fd (sys tcp listen \"127.0.0.1\" 0 64)) (limites)\n        r1 = una vuelta (una vuelta r0)\n        s  = reactor stats r1\n        echo \"abiertas {open_count s}, rechazadas {refused_count s}, cerradas por un límite {dropped_count s}\"\n        echo (accepted_count (reactor stop r1 500))\n```\n\n### 32.3.3. Ejemplo 3: Aceptar hasta un límite por vuelta, rechazar con la tabla llena e identificadores que no se repiten\n\n\n\n```ridgun\nfn :: test reactor accepts and refuses => ()\n      test reactor accepts and refuses =\n        d = reactor defaults\n        max_conn_count d -> assert int equals 1024 \"defaults: 1 024 connections\"\n        max_accept_count d -> assert int equals 64 \"64 accepted in a turn\"\n        input_limit_bytes d -> assert int equals 67108864 \"64 MB of input\"\n        output_limit_bytes d -> assert int equals 67108864 \"64 MB of output\"\n        first_message_limit_ms d -> assert int equals 0 \"no limit for the first message\"\n        idle_limit_ms d -> assert int equals 0 \"no idle limit\"\n        max_conn_count (reactor with max conns d 0) -> assert int equals 1 \"a table holds at least one connection\"\n\n        lfd = na listen\n        r0  = na start lfd (reactor with max accepts (reactor with max conns d 2) 2)\n        e0  = na turn r0 20\n        na count (reactor arrived e0) 0 -> assert int equals 0 \"nobody connected: nothing arrived\"\n        open_count (reactor stats e0) -> assert int equals 0 \"and the table is empty\"\n\n        c1 = na client lfd\n        c2 = na client lfd\n        c3 = na client lfd\n        r1 = na turn r0 500\n        na same (reactor arrived r1) [1, 2] -> assert true \"AC1: three are pending and a turn accepts two, with ids from 1\"\n        reactor peer r1 1 -> assert str eq \"127.0.0.1\" \"AC1: the address of the peer\"\n        reactor peer r1 99 -> assert str eq \"\" \"an id that is not in the table has no peer\"\n        open_count (reactor stats r1) -> assert int equals 2 \"AC12: two open\"\n        accepted_count (reactor stats r1) -> assert int equals 2 \"AC12: two accepted\"\n        r2 = na turn r1 500\n        na count (reactor arrived r2) 0 -> assert int equals 0 \"AC2: the table is full, the third does not enter\"\n        refused_count (reactor stats r2) -> assert int equals 1 \"AC2: and it is counted as refused\"\n        open_count (reactor stats r2) -> assert int equals 2 \"AC2: the two in the table are still there\"\n        na recv rc (sys recv c3 16 500) -> assert int equals (0 - 1) \"AC2: the refused client sees its connection closed\"\n\n        posix close c1\n        r3 = na turn r2 500\n        na same (reactor left r3) [1] -> assert true \"AC3: a connection closed by its peer leaves the table\"\n        open_count (reactor stats r3) -> assert int equals 1 \"one open\"\n        c4 = na client lfd\n        r4 = na turn r3 500\n        na same (reactor arrived r4) [3] -> assert true \"AC1: an id is never given again: the next one is 3\"\n        na count (reactor left r4) 0 -> assert int equals 0 \"what left is of the last turn only\"\n        accepted_count (reactor stats r4) -> assert int equals 3 \"three accepted in all\"\n        dropped_count (reactor stats r4) -> assert int equals 0 \"none closed for a limit\"\n        st = reactor stop r4 200\n        open_count st -> assert int equals 0 \"after the stop nothing is open\"\n        posix close c2\n        posix close c3\n        posix close c4 -> ()\n```\n\n### 32.3.4. Ejemplo 4: Un mensaje que llega a trozos, el estado de cada conexión y un protocolo de líneas con `reactor each`\n\n\n\n```ridgun\nfn :: test reactor input messages and state => ()\n      test reactor input messages and state =\n        lfd = na listen\n        r0  = na start lfd (reactor defaults)\n        c1  = na client lfd\n        r1  = na turn r0 500\n        na same (reactor arrived r1) [1] -> assert true \"one connection\"\n        na count (reactor ready r1) 0 -> assert int equals 0 \"it has sent nothing: not ready\"\n        sock rc (sys send c1 \"hel\" 500) -> assert int equals 0 \"the client sends a part\"\n        r2  = na turn r1 500\n        na same (reactor ready r2) [1] -> assert true \"AC3: its bytes are in the input\"\n        reactor input r2 1 -> assert str eq \"hel\" \"AC3: the input\"\n        r3  = reactor take r2 1 0\n        reactor input r3 1 -> assert str eq \"hel\" \"AC4: nothing taken, the bytes stay\"\n        sock rc (sys send c1 \"lo\\nwor\" 500) -> assert int equals 0 \"the rest of the message and the start of another\"\n        r4  = na turn r3 500\n        reactor input r4 1 -> assert str eq \"hello\\nwor\" \"AC4: a message that came in two reads is whole, once\"\n        r5  = reactor take r4 1 6\n        reactor input r5 1 -> assert str eq \"wor\" \"AC4: the message is taken and the rest stays\"\n        r6  = na turn r5 30\n        reactor input r6 1 -> assert str eq \"wor\" \"AC4: and it is still there a turn later\"\n        sock rc (sys send c1 \"ld\\n\" 500) -> assert int equals 0 \"the end of the second message\"\n        r7  = na turn r6 500\n        reactor input r7 1 -> assert str eq \"world\\n\" \"AC4: offered again with what arrived later\"\n        r8  = reactor take r7 1 100\n        reactor input r8 1 -> assert str eq \"\" \"taking more than there is takes it all\"\n        reactor input r8 77 -> assert str eq \"\" \"an id that is not in the table has no input\"\n\n        -- AC10: the state of each connection\n        reactor state r8 1 5 -> assert int equals 5 \"AC10: no state left yet: the default\"\n        r9  = reactor set state r8 1 41\n        reactor state r9 1 5 -> assert int equals 41 \"AC10: the state that was left\"\n        c2  = na client lfd\n        r10 = na turn r9 500\n        reactor state r10 2 5 -> assert int equals 5 \"AC10: another connection has its own\"\n        reactor state r10 1 5 -> assert int equals 41 \"AC10: and the first one keeps its state\"\n        open_count (reactor stats (reactor set state r10 99 1)) -> assert int equals 2 \"an operation on an id that is not there changes nothing\"\n\n        -- reactor each: a protocol of lines\n        l0  = na start (na listen) (reactor defaults)\n        d1  = na client (rx_fd l0)\n        d2  = na client (rx_fd l0)\n        l1  = na turn l0 500\n        sock rc (sys send d1 \"a\\nb\\npart\" 500) -> assert int equals 0 \"two lines and a part\"\n        sock rc (sys send d2 \"x\\n\" 500) -> assert int equals 0 \"the other client, one line\"\n        l2  = reactor each (na turns l1 2 100) 0 (na line step)\n        reactor input l2 1 -> assert str eq \"b\\npart\" \"each: one call for each connection, it took one line\"\n        reactor state l2 1 0 -> assert int equals 1 \"each: the state it left\"\n        l3  = reactor each l2 0 (na line step)\n        reactor input l3 1 -> assert str eq \"part\" \"each: the second line; the part stays\"\n        reactor state l3 1 0 -> assert int equals 2 \"each: its state after two lines\"\n        reactor state l3 2 0 -> assert int equals 1 \"each: the other connection has its own count\"\n        l4  = reactor each l3 0 (na line step)\n        reactor state l4 1 0 -> assert int equals 2 \"each: no whole line, nothing changes\"\n        p1  = na pump l4 d1 8 40 \"\"\n        na pumped text p1 -> assert str eq \"1:a\\n2:b\\n\" \"AC5: the answers leave in the order they were queued\"\n        p2  = na pump (na pumped r p1) d2 4 40 \"\"\n        na pumped text p2 -> assert str eq \"1:x\\n\" \"each connection gets its own answer\"\n        sock rc (sys send d1 \"ial\\nquit\\n\" 500) -> assert int equals 0 \"the rest of the line, and quit\"\n        l5  = reactor each (na turns (na pumped r p2) 2 100) 0 (na line step)\n        l6  = reactor each l5 0 (na line step)\n        p3  = na pump l6 d1 11 40 \"\"\n        na pumped text p3 -> assert str eq \"3:partial\\nbye\\n\" \"the line that came in two parts is answered once, whole\"\n        l7  = na turns (na pumped r p3) 3 50\n        na recv rc (sys recv d1 16 500) -> assert int equals (0 - 1) \"AC7: after the answer to quit the client sees the end\"\n        open_count (reactor stats l7) -> assert int equals 2 \"the reactor waits for the client to close its side\"\n        posix close d1\n        l8  = na turns l7 3 50\n        open_count (reactor stats l8) -> assert int equals 1 \"AC7: and then the connection leaves the table\"\n        dropped_count (reactor stats l8) -> assert int equals 0 \"not counted as closed for a limit\"\n        reactor stop l8 100\n        reactor stop r10 100\n        posix close c1\n        posix close c2\n        posix close d2 -> ()\n```\n\n### 32.3.5. Ejemplo 5: La salida en orden, una respuesta grande en varias vueltas y el par que no lee\n\n\n\n```ridgun\nfn :: test reactor output and the peer that does not read => ()\n      test reactor output and the peer that does not read =\n        lfd  = na listen\n        r0   = na start lfd (reactor with output limit (reactor defaults) 3000000)\n        slow = na client lfd\n        fast = na client lfd\n        r1   = na turn r0 500\n        na same (reactor arrived r1) [1, 2] -> assert true \"two connections\"\n        big  = na text 2000000\n        r2   = reactor send (reactor send r1 2 \"one\") 2 \"two\"\n        p0   = na pump r2 fast 6 40 \"\"\n        na pumped text p0 -> assert str eq \"onetwo\" \"AC5: what was queued leaves in its order\"\n\n        -- AC5: a reply larger than the socket takes at once goes out over several turns, whole\n        r3   = reactor send (na pumped r p0) 2 big\n        p1   = na pump r3 fast 2000000 4000 \"\"\n        str len (na pumped text p1) -> assert int equals 2000000 \"AC5: two million bytes arrive\"\n        (na pumped text p1) == big -> assert true \"AC5: and they are the bytes that were queued\"\n\n        -- AC6: the peer that does not read does not delay the others\n        r4   = reactor send (na pumped r p1) 1 big\n        t0   = sys monotonic ms\n        r5   = na turns r4 5 20\n        (sys monotonic ms) - t0 < 1500 -> assert true \"AC6: five turns with a peer that does not read do not wait for it\"\n        open_count (reactor stats r5) -> assert int equals 2 \"under the limit it stays, with its output queued\"\n        r6   = reactor send r5 2 \"still here\"\n        p2   = na pump r6 fast 10 40 \"\"\n        na pumped text p2 -> assert str eq \"still here\" \"AC6: the other connection is served meanwhile\"\n        r7   = reactor send (na pumped r p2) 1 (big + big + big + big + big + big)\n        r8   = na turns r7 3 20\n        na same (reactor left r8) [] -> assert true \"left is of the last turn\"\n        dropped_count (reactor stats r8) -> assert int equals 1 \"AC6: past the output limit the connection is closed and counted\"\n        open_count (reactor stats r8) -> assert int equals 1 \"AC6: and only that one\"\n        r9   = reactor send r8 2 \"after\"\n        p3   = na pump r9 fast 5 40 \"\"\n        na pumped text p3 -> assert str eq \"after\" \"the other connection goes on\"\n\n        -- AC7: marked to close: its output is sent first, and nothing more is read from it\n        c3   = na client lfd\n        r10  = na turn (na pumped r p3) 500\n        na same (reactor arrived r10) [3] -> assert true \"a third connection\"\n        r11  = reactor close after send (reactor send r10 3 (na text 1500000)) 3\n        sock rc (sys send c3 \"ignored\" 500) -> assert int equals 0 \"the client sends after it was marked\"\n        r12  = na turns r11 3 20\n        reactor input r12 3 -> assert str eq \"\" \"AC7: nothing is read from a connection marked to close\"\n        p4   = na pump r12 c3 1500000 4000 \"\"\n        str len (na pumped text p4) -> assert int equals 1500000 \"AC7: its queued output is sent whole\"\n        r13a = na turns (na pumped r p4) 3 50\n        na recv rc (sys recv c3 16 500) -> assert int equals (0 - 1) \"AC7: and then the client sees the end, with nothing lost\"\n        posix close c3\n        r13  = na turns r13a 3 50\n        open_count (reactor stats r13) -> assert int equals 1 \"it left the table\"\n        dropped_count (reactor stats r13) -> assert int equals 1 \"and was not counted as closed for a limit\"\n\n        -- a client that never closes its side: the reactor closes it after waiting one second\n        c5   = na client lfd\n        r14  = na turn r13 500\n        r15  = reactor close after send (reactor send r14 4 \"end\") 4\n        r16  = na turns r15 3 50\n        na read c5 500 -> assert str eq \"end\" \"the last output arrives\"\n        open_count (reactor stats r16) -> assert int equals 2 \"the client has not closed: the connection waits\"\n        r17  = na turns r16 14 100\n        open_count (reactor stats r17) -> assert int equals 1 \"AC7: after one second the reactor closes it anyway\"\n\n        -- AC3: the input limit\n        l2   = na start (na listen) (reactor with input limit (reactor defaults) 1000)\n        c4   = na client (rx_fd l2)\n        l3   = na turn l2 500\n        sock rc (sys send c4 (na text 5000) 500) -> assert int equals 0 \"five thousand bytes into a limit of one thousand\"\n        l4   = na turns l3 2 100\n        dropped_count (reactor stats l4) -> assert int equals 1 \"AC3: past the input limit the connection is closed and counted\"\n        open_count (reactor stats l4) -> assert int equals 0 \"and leaves the table\"\n        reactor stop l4 100\n        reactor stop r17 100\n        posix close slow\n        posix close fast\n        posix close c4\n        posix close c5 -> ()\n```\n\n### 32.3.6. Ejemplo 6: El tiempo para el primer mensaje y el tiempo de inactividad\n\n\n\n```ridgun\nfn :: test reactor time limits => ()\n      test reactor time limits =\n        lfd = na listen\n        r0  = na start lfd (reactor with first message limit (reactor defaults) 150)\n        c1  = na client lfd\n        c2  = na client lfd\n        r1  = na turn r0 500\n        sock rc (sys send c2 \"msg\\n\" 500) -> assert int equals 0 \"the second sends its first message\"\n        r2  = reactor take (na turn r1 500) 2 4\n        r3  = na turns r2 6 60\n        dropped_count (reactor stats r3) -> assert int equals 1 \"AC8: the one that sent no whole message in 150 ms is closed\"\n        open_count (reactor stats r3) -> assert int equals 1 \"AC8: the one whose message was taken stays\"\n        na recv rc (sys recv c1 16 500) -> assert int equals (0 - 1) \"the silent client sees the close\"\n        reactor stop r3 100\n\n        l0  = na start (na listen) (reactor with idle limit (reactor defaults) 150)\n        d1  = na client (rx_fd l0)\n        l1  = na turn l0 500\n        sock rc (sys send d1 \"hi\" 500) -> assert int equals 0 \"it sends\"\n        l2  = na turns l1 2 40\n        open_count (reactor stats l2) -> assert int equals 1 \"AC8: active within the idle limit: it stays\"\n        l3  = na turns l2 6 60\n        dropped_count (reactor stats l3) -> assert int equals 1 \"AC8: silent for longer than the idle limit: closed\"\n        open_count (reactor stats l3) -> assert int equals 0 \"and gone from the table\"\n        reactor stop l3 100\n        posix close c1\n        posix close c2\n        posix close d1 -> ()\n```\n\n### 32.3.7. Ejemplo 7: Una sola espera sobre todo: conexiones, una tubería del llamador y un pool de trabajadores\n\n\n\n```ridgun\nfn :: test reactor waits on everything at once => ()\n      test reactor waits on everything at once =\n        lfd = na listen\n        r0  = na start lfd (reactor defaults)\n        pp  = posix pipe\n        pr  = tuple3 r pp\n        pw  = tuple3 w pp\n\n        -- AC9: nothing happens: the turn sleeps for its limit and answers nothing\n        t0  = sys monotonic ms\n        a0  = reactor turn r0 [pr] 120\n        t1  = sys monotonic ms\n        na count (na second a0) 0 -> assert int equals 0 \"AC9: nothing ready\"\n        (t1 - t0) >= 100 -> assert true \"AC9: the turn slept for its limit, it did not spin\"\n        (t1 - t0) < 1500 -> assert true \"and not much longer\"\n\n        -- a descriptor of the caller wakes it\n        posix write pw \"x\" -> assert int equals 1 \"a byte in the pipe\"\n        t2  = sys monotonic ms\n        a1  = reactor turn (na first a0) [pr] 5000\n        na same (na second a1) [pr] -> assert true \"AC9: the descriptor of the caller is named as ready\"\n        (sys monotonic ms) - t2 < 1000 -> assert true \"AC9: and the turn returned at once, not after 5 s\"\n\n        -- a connection wakes it\n        c1  = na client lfd\n        t3  = sys monotonic ms\n        a2  = reactor turn (na first a1) [] 5000\n        na same (reactor arrived (na first a2)) [1] -> assert true \"AC9: a new connection wakes the turn\"\n        (sys monotonic ms) - t3 < 1000 -> assert true \"at once\"\n        sock rc (sys send c1 \"data\" 500) -> assert int equals 0 \"the client sends\"\n        t4  = sys monotonic ms\n        a3  = reactor turn (na first a2) [] 5000\n        reactor input (na first a3) 1 -> assert str eq \"data\" \"AC9: bytes on a connection wake the turn\"\n        (sys monotonic ms) - t4 < 1000 -> assert true \"at once\"\n\n        -- the descriptor of a worker pool\n        p0  = pool start 1 (na slow double) 0\n        k, p1 = pool submit p0 21 \"\"\n        a4  = reactor turn (na first a3) [pool done fd p1] 5000\n        na same (na second a4) [pool done fd p1] -> assert true \"AC9: the turn waits on the descriptor of a worker pool and names it when a job ends\"\n        done, p2 = pool drain p1 1000\n        reactor stop (na first a4) 100\n        posix close pr\n        posix close pw\n        posix close c1 -> ()\n```\n\n### 32.3.8. Ejemplo 8: La parada: se envía lo encolado y se cierra todo\n\n\n\n```ridgun\nfn :: test reactor stop => ()\n      test reactor stop =\n        lfd  = na listen\n        port = sys local port lfd\n        r0   = na start lfd (reactor defaults)\n        c1   = na client lfd\n        c2   = na client lfd\n        r1   = na turn r0 500\n        r2   = reactor send (reactor send r1 1 \"last words one\") 2 \"last words two\"\n        st   = reactor stop r2 1000\n        open_count st -> assert int equals 0 \"AC11: after the stop nothing is open\"\n        accepted_count st -> assert int equals 2 \"AC12: the counters at the end\"\n        na read c1 500 -> assert str eq \"last words one\" \"AC11: the queued output was sent before closing\"\n        na read c2 500 -> assert str eq \"last words two\" \"AC11: to each connection\"\n        na recv rc (sys recv c1 16 500) -> assert int equals (0 - 1) \"AC11: and the connections are closed\"\n        sock rc (sys tcp connect \"127.0.0.1\" port 300) != 0 -> assert true \"AC11: the listening socket is closed: nobody can connect\"\n\n        -- a peer that does not read does not hold the stop longer than its time\n        l0   = na start (na listen) (reactor defaults)\n        d1   = na client (rx_fd l0)\n        l1   = reactor send (na turn l0 500) 1 (na text 3000000)\n        t0   = sys monotonic ms\n        s2   = reactor stop l1 300\n        (sys monotonic ms) - t0 < 2000 -> assert true \"AC11: the stop ends at its time limit\"\n        open_count s2 -> assert int equals 0 \"and everything is closed\"\n        posix close c1\n        posix close c2\n        posix close d1 -> ()\n```\n\n---\n\n## 32.4. Bajo el capó: cómo está construida `net_agent` en Ridgun puro (`src/main/ridgun/lib/net_agent.ridgun`)\n\nUna de las mayores ventajas de `ridgun-libs` es que **no hay cajas negras en C**. Puedes abrir `src/main/ridgun/lib/net_agent.ridgun` y leer exactamente cómo está implementada cada operación usando *pattern matching*, árboles de guardas `|` / `|.` y recursión de cola (TCO). Veamos las piezas clave de su implementación real:\n\n### 32.4.1. Implementación interna: Accepting (AC1, AC2)\n\nFíjate en cómo `net_agent.ridgun` estructura las firmas `fn :: ... => ...` primero y resuelve cada caso mediante ecuaciones alineadas y llamadas de cola:\n\n```ridgun\nmodule :: net_agent\n\n-- The table is full: the new connection is closed at once and counted.\nfn :: rx refuse (Reactor S) Int => Reactor S\n      rx refuse r           fd  =\n        closed = posix close fd\n        r with rx_refused = (rx_refused r) + 1\n\nfn :: rx admit (Reactor S) Int String Int => Reactor S\n      rx admit r           fd  ip     now =\n        r with rx_conns = (rx_conns r) :: [ReactorConn (rx_next r) fd ip \"\" \"\" False now now False False []], rx_next = (rx_next r) + 1, rx_arrived = (rx_arrived r) :: [rx_next r], rx_accepted = (rx_accepted r) + 1\n\nfn :: rx accept one (Reactor S) Int Int (Int Int String) => Reactor S\n      rx accept one r           now left (rc, fd, ip)    =\n        | rc != 0                                                  = r\n        | (rx count (rx_conns r) 0) >= (max_conn_count (rx_cfg r)) = rx accept some (rx refuse r fd) now (left - 1)\n        | otherwise                                                = rx accept some (rx admit r fd ip now) now (left - 1)\n\n-- Accepts those that are pending, without waiting, at most `left` of them.\nfn :: rx accept some (Reactor S) Int Int => Reactor S\n      rx accept some r           now left =\n        | left <= 0 = r\n        | otherwise = rx accept one r now left (sys accept (rx_fd r) 0)\n\nfn :: rx accept all (Reactor S) WaitMany Int => Reactor S\n      rx accept all r           w        now =\n        | (rx_fd r) < 0                      = r\n        | not (rx has (wm_read w) (rx_fd r)) = r\n        | otherwise                          = rx accept some r now (max_accept_count (rx_cfg r))\n```\n\n### 32.4.2. Implementación interna: Reading, sending and the limits (AC3, AC5, AC6, AC7, AC8)\n\nFíjate en cómo `net_agent.ridgun` estructura las firmas `fn :: ... => ...` primero y resuelve cada caso mediante ecuaciones alineadas y llamadas de cola:\n\n```ridgun\n-- Each step answers a kind with the connection: 0 it stays, 1 it leaves (its peer closed, it failed, or it\n-- was marked to close and its output is sent), 2 it leaves for passing a limit.\n\nfn :: rx read got (ReactorConn S) Int (Int String) => Int (ReactorConn S)\n      rx read got c               now (rc, data)   =\n        | rc == 0       = (0, c with cn_in = (cn_in c) + data, cn_active = now)\n        | rc == (0 - 2) = (0, c)\n        | otherwise     = (1, c)\n\n-- A connection that only waits for its peer to close: what arrives is thrown away; the end of the peer ends it.\nfn :: rx drain got (ReactorConn S) (Int String) => Int (ReactorConn S)\n      rx drain got c               (rc, data)   =\n        | rc == 0       = (0, c)\n        | rc == (0 - 2) = (0, c)\n        | otherwise     = (1, c)\n\n-- What has arrived is added to the input, without waiting. A closing connection is not read.\nfn :: rx read step (ReactorConn S) WaitMany Int => Int (ReactorConn S)\n      rx read step c               w        now =\n        | not (rx has (wm_read w) (cn_fd c)) = (0, c)\n        | cn_done c                          = rx drain got c (sys recv (cn_fd c) 65536 0)\n        | cn_closing c                       = (0, c)\n        | otherwise                          = rx read got c now (sys recv (cn_fd c) 65536 0)\n\nfn :: rx write got (ReactorConn S) Int (Int Int) => Int (ReactorConn S)\n      rx write got c               now (rc, sent) =\n        | rc == 0                    = (0, c with cn_out = \"\", cn_active = now)\n        | rc == (0 - 2) and sent > 0 = (0, c with cn_out = (str slice (cn_out c) sent (str len (cn_out c))), cn_active = now)\n        | rc == (0 - 2)              = (0, c)\n        | otherwise                  = (1, c)\n\n-- The peer is sent what it takes now; the rest stays queued, in its order.\nfn :: rx write step (Int (ReactorConn S)) WaitMany Int => Int (ReactorConn S)\n      rx write step (kind, c)             w        now =\n        | kind != 0                           = (kind, c)\n        | (str len (cn_out c)) == 0           = (0, c)\n        | not (rx has (wm_write w) (cn_fd c)) = (0, c)\n        | otherwise                           = rx write got c now (sys send (cn_fd c) (cn_out c) 0)\n\nfn :: rx over Int   Int   => Bool\n      rx over limit spent =  (limit > 0) and (spent > limit)\n\n-- How long a connection whose output is all sent waits for its peer to close before it is closed anyway.\nfn :: rx linger ms => Int\n      rx linger ms =  1000\n\n-- The output of a closing connection is all sent: its sending side is shut, so the peer sees the end after the\n-- last byte. The connection is not closed yet: closing a socket that still holds bytes the peer sent makes the\n-- kernel cut the connection, and the peer can lose output it had not read.\nfn :: rx shut sending (ReactorConn S) Int Int => Int (ReactorConn S)\n      rx shut sending c               now _   =  (0, c with cn_done = True, cn_active = now)\n\nfn :: rx after io ReactorConfig (Int (ReactorConn S)) Int => Int (ReactorConn S)\n      rx after io cfg           (kind, c)             now =\n        | kind != 0                                                                        = (kind, c)\n        | (cn_done c) and ((now - (cn_active c)) > (rx linger ms))                         = (1, c)\n        | cn_done c                                                                        = (0, c)\n        | (cn_closing c) and ((str len (cn_out c)) == 0)                                   = rx shut sending c now (sys shutdown write (cn_fd c))\n        | (str len (cn_in c)) > (input_limit_bytes cfg)                                    = (2, c)\n        | (str len (cn_out c)) > (output_limit_bytes cfg)                                  = (2, c)\n        | (not (cn_first c)) and (rx over (first_message_limit_ms cfg) (now - (cn_since c))) = (2, c)\n        | rx over (idle_limit_ms cfg) (now - (cn_active c))                                = (2, c)\n        | otherwise                                                                        = (0, c)\n\nfn :: rx serve one ReactorConfig (ReactorConn S) WaitMany Int => Int (ReactorConn S)\n      rx serve one cfg           c               w        now =\n        | rx has (wm_failed w) (cn_fd c) = (1, c)\n        | otherwise                      = rx after io cfg (rx write step (rx read step c w now) w now) now\n\nfn :: rx serve each ReactorConfig [(ReactorConn S)] WaitMany Int => [Int (ReactorConn S)]\n      rx serve each cfg           []                w        now =  []\n      rx serve each cfg           (c:rest)          w        now =  [rx serve one cfg c w now] :: (rx serve each cfg rest w now)\n\n-- The connections that stay.\nfn :: rx kept [Int (ReactorConn S)] => [(ReactorConn S)]\n      rx kept []                    =  []\n      rx kept ((kind, c):rest)      =\n        | kind == 0 = [c] :: (rx kept rest)\n        | otherwise = rx kept rest\n\n-- The ids of the connections that leave; each one is closed here, once.\nfn :: rx gone [Int (ReactorConn S)] => [Int]\n      rx gone []                    =  []\n      rx gone ((kind, c):rest)      =\n        | kind == 0 = rx gone rest\n        | otherwise = rx gone closed c (posix close (cn_fd c)) rest\n\nfn :: rx gone closed (ReactorConn S) Int [Int (ReactorConn S)] => [Int]\n      rx gone closed c               _   rest                  =  [cn_id c] :: (rx gone rest)\n\nfn :: rx limit count [Int (ReactorConn S)] Int => Int\n      rx limit count []                    n   =  n\n      rx limit count ((kind, c):rest)      n   =\n        | kind == 2 = rx limit count rest (n + 1)\n        | otherwise = rx limit count rest n\n\nfn :: rx serve done (Reactor S) [Int (ReactorConn S)] => Reactor S\n      rx serve done r           served                =\n        r with rx_conns = (rx kept served), rx_left = (rx gone served), rx_dropped = (rx_dropped r) + (rx limit count served 0)\n```\n\n### 32.4.3. Implementación interna: One turn (AC9)\n\nFíjate en cómo `net_agent.ridgun` estructura las firmas `fn :: ... => ...` primero y resuelve cada caso mediante ecuaciones alineadas y llamadas de cola:\n\n```ridgun\n-- One turn of the loop. It waits at most `timeout_ms` for the listening socket, every connection and the\n-- descriptors of the caller in `extra` (a signal descriptor, the descriptor of a worker pool): one wait on all\n-- of them. Then it accepts, reads, sends and applies the limits, without waiting for any connection.\n-- The answer is the reactor to use from now on and the descriptors of `extra` that are ready.\nfn :: reactor turn (Reactor S) [Int] Int        => (Reactor S) [Int]\n      reactor turn r           extra timeout_ms =\n        w   = posix wait many ((rx listen fds (rx_fd r)) :: ((rx read fds (rx_conns r)) :: extra)) (rx write fds (rx_conns r)) timeout_ms\n        now = sys monotonic ms\n        r1  = rx accept all (r with rx_arrived = [], rx_left = []) w now\n        r2  = rx serve done r1 (rx serve each (rx_cfg r1) (rx_conns r1) w now)\n        (r2, rx pick ready extra (wm_read w))\n```\n\n### 32.4.4. Implementación interna: Stop (AC11)\n\nFíjate en cómo `net_agent.ridgun` estructura las firmas `fn :: ... => ...` primero y resuelve cada caso mediante ecuaciones alineadas y llamadas de cola:\n\n```ridgun\nfn :: rx all closing [(ReactorConn S)] => [(ReactorConn S)]\n      rx all closing []                =  []\n      rx all closing (c:rest)          =  [c with cn_closing = True] :: (rx all closing rest)\n\nfn :: rx close fds [(ReactorConn S)] Int => Int\n      rx close fds []                n   =  n\n      rx close fds (c:rest)          n   =  rx close fds rest (n + (rx at most (posix close (cn_fd c)) 0) + 1)\n\nfn :: rx stop listening (Reactor S) => Reactor S\n      rx stop listening r           =\n        | (rx_fd r) < 0 = r\n        | otherwise     = rx stopped listening r (posix close (rx_fd r))\n\nfn :: rx stopped listening (Reactor S) Int => Reactor S\n      rx stopped listening r           _   =  r with rx_fd = (0 - 1)\n\nfn :: rx turn only ((Reactor S) [Int]) => Reactor S\n      rx turn only (r, _)              =  r\n\nfn :: rx stop end (Reactor S) => ReactorStats\n      rx stop end r           =\n        n = rx close fds (rx_conns r) 0\n        ReactorStats 0 (rx_accepted r) (rx_refused r) (rx_dropped r)\n\n-- Turns that only send, until nothing is queued or the time ends.\nfn :: rx stop flush (Reactor S) Int      => ReactorStats\n      rx stop flush r           deadline =\n        | (rx count (rx_conns r) 0) == 0 = rx stop end r\n        | (sys monotonic ms) >= deadline = rx stop end r\n        | otherwise                      = rx stop flush (rx turn only (reactor turn r [] (rx at most (deadline - (sys monotonic ms)) 50))) deadline\n\n-- Stops the reactor: no more connections are accepted, the queued output is sent for at most `timeout_ms`,\n-- and every connection and the listening socket are closed. The answer is the counters at the end.\nfn :: reactor stop (Reactor S) Int        => ReactorStats\n      reactor stop r           timeout_ms =\n        s = rx stop listening r\n        rx stop flush (s with rx_conns = (rx all closing (rx_conns s))) ((sys monotonic ms) + (rx at least timeout_ms 0))\n```\n\n---\n\n## 32.5. Garantías algorítmicas, memoria `RMM1`/`RMM2` y las 5 Reglas de Oro de `net_agent`\n\n- **Garantía algorítmica y de seguridad**: Ninguna conexión hace esperar a otra: la única espera de una vuelta es una sola espera sobre todos los descriptores a la vez. La tabla, la entrada y la salida retenidas por conexión, el tiempo para su primer mensaje y su tiempo de inactividad están acotados, y una conexión que pasa un límite se cierra y se cuenta. Una conexión marcada para cerrar se cierra de forma ordenada, de modo que su par no pierde salida.\n- **Complejidad de pila $O(1)$ con TCO**: Todos los bucles recursivos en `src/main/ridgun/lib/net_agent.ridgun` están en posición de cola, por lo que `ridgunc` los compila a saltos nativos sin crecimiento de pila.\n- **Memoria determinista (`RMM1`/`RMM2`)**: Cero pausas de recolector de basura; todas las estructuras intermedias se liberan de forma determinista al salir del ámbito.\n- **Verificación continua**: Probada exhaustivamente con `stable check` y la suite automatizada `src/test/ridgun/test net_agent.ridgun`.\n\n### Las 5 Reglas de Oro al programar con `net_agent`\n\n1. **Declara `import net_agent` al inicio del archivo** y llama a sus funciones con espacios, tal como están declaradas, para que tu código se lea como prosa.\n2. **Alinea tus tuberías de datos con `=`**: encadena las llamadas a `net_agent` en pasos con nombre propio y deja que `stable format` alinee las columnas.\n3. **Aprovecha las funciones totales de `net_agent` en tus guardas `|`**: comprueba los valores de retorno o desenvuelve los ADTs con *pattern matching* en lugar de asumir que la entrada externa siempre es válida.\n4. **Evita copiar grandes estructuras si solo necesitas consultar un campo**: recuerda que en `RMM2` los argumentos de entrada no incrementan ni decrementan contadores (`+0` / `-0`).\n5. **Combina `net_agent` con `test` (`import test`)**: escribe siempre aserciones con `assert equals` o `assert true` para fijar los invariantes de tu dominio.\n\n---\n\nEn el **Capítulo 33** pasaremos a explorar en profundidad la lib **`ai`** (La lib `ai` — Agentes de IA, Tool Calling, Streaming SSE, ReAct Acotado, Guardarraíles, Mini-RAG y MCP).\n"}, {"num": "32", "slug": "33-lib-ai-agentes-ia-herramientas-streaming-rag-y-mcp", "file": "33-lib-ai-agentes-ia-herramientas-streaming-rag-y-mcp.md", "title": "Capítulo 33: La lib `ai` — Agentes de IA, Tool Calling, Streaming SSE, ReAct Acotado, Guardarraíles, Mini-RAG y MCP", "short_title": "La lib `ai` — Agentes de IA, Tool Calling, Streaming SSE, ReAct Acotado, Guardarraíles, Mini-RAG y MCP", "markdown": "# Capítulo 33: La lib `ai` — Agentes de IA, Tool Calling, Streaming SSE, ReAct Acotado, Guardarraíles, Mini-RAG y MCP\n\n## 33.1. ¿Por qué existe la lib `ai`? (El problema real y la filosofía Ridgun)\n\n> *«¿Por qué necesito una lib `ai` escrita desde cero en Ridgun puro si ya tengo actores nativos (`agent`) y cliente HTTP (`http`)?»*\n\nPorque en Ridgun `agent` es la primitiva de concurrencia del lenguaje (buzones, mensajes y aislamiento de memoria), mientras que **`ai`** es la inteligencia cognitiva y el protocolo determinista que convierte un actor en un **Agente de IA en producción**:\n\n1. **Conversaciones inmutables, separación de `...` y compactación de contexto (`ai compact conv`)**: los modelos razonadores (*DeepSeek-R1*, *Qwen-QwQ*, *Claude Thinking*) emiten bloques `` que no deben reenviarse en turnos posteriores para no agotar la ventana de contexto. `ai split thinking`, `ai strip thinking`, `ai trim context` y `ai compact conv` mantienen el historial limpio y acotado.\n2. **Esquemas declarativos de herramientas (`AiTool`) y codecs multi-proveedor (OpenAI, Anthropic, Ollama y XML ``)**: defines tus herramientas una sola vez con `ai tool` y `ai param`, validas llamadas antes de ejecutarlas con `ai validate tool call`, y codificas/parseas peticiones y respuestas sin acoplarte a un único proveedor.\n3. **Streaming SSE incremental (`AiStreamAcc`) y auto-reparación de salidas estructuradas (`ai extract json`, `ai build repair prompt`)**: reensambla fragmentos `data:` de Server-Sent Events en tiempo real y extrae JSON limpio aunque el LLM lo envuelva en bloques Markdown ```` ```json ```` o texto conversacional.\n4. **Máquina de estados ReAct acotada (`AiPolicy`, `ai step`), caché determinista de replay (`ai replay lookup`), guardarraíles de seguridad (`ai wrap untrusted`, `ai has injection pattern`, `ai scrub secrets`), Mini-RAG en memoria (`ai retrieve top k`) y cliente MCP JSON-RPC 2.0 (`ai mcp tools call req`)**: evita bucles infinitos y sobrecostes de tokens, redacta claves filtradas (`sk-`, `ghp_`, `AKIA`, `Bearer `), puntúa documentos por solapamiento léxico y conecta con servidores *Model Context Protocol* (MCP).\n\n---\n\n## 33.2. budget exceeded\" \"AC6: max_tokens diagnostic\"\n\n        AiReply \"quietClean final answer\" (AiUsage 10 15 25) -> turn_done\n        ai step c0 turn_done pol -> step_done\n        assert true (dec "# Capítulo 34: La lib `locale` — Reglas de Plurales CLDR, Formato UTC de Fechas y Números y Autónimos\n\n## 34.1. ¿Por qué existe la lib `locale`? (El problema real y la filosofía Ridgun)\n\n> *«¿Por qué necesito una lib `locale` escrita desde cero en Ridgun puro en lugar de depender de `setlocale()` de `libc` o arrastrar 30 MB de `libicu`?»*\n\nEn sistemas reales (como pasarelas i18n, plantillas multilingües y motores de catálogos `.po` al estilo de `babel`), `setlocale()` en C muta estado global compartido entre hilos y `libicu` rompe cualquier despliegue ligero. La lib **`locale`** (`src/main/ridgun/lib/locale.ridgun`, dominio `LOCALE`) incorpora directamente en Ridgun puro las tablas **Unicode CLDR 46** y el calendario civil UTC en $O(1)$ de Howard Hinnant:\n\n1. **Reglas de plurales CLDR en doble modo (`.po` 2 formas por defecto + CLDR 46 estricto con `\"many\"`)**: `plural category` y `plural index` ofrecen por defecto el modo compatible con catálogos Gettext `.po` (`[\"one\", \"other\"]` para `es`, `ca`, `gl`, `eu`, `en`, `pt`, `sv`, `it`, `de`, `nl`; regla `n == 0 or n == 1` para `fr`; 3 formas eslavas para `ru`, `uk`, `pl`; 6 formas para `ar`; invariante para `ja`, `zh`, `ko`), mientras `plural category cldr` y `plural categories cldr` activan la categoría `\"many\"` de CLDR 46 para millones exactos (`1000000`, `2000000`...) en `es`, `ca`, `pt`, `it` y `fr`.\n2. **Formateo de fechas y marcas temporales UTC (`format date`, `format datetime`, `month name`, `weekday name`)**: convierte segundos Unix epoch mediante el algoritmo civil de Howard Hinnant en $O(1)$ y aplica los patrones `short`, `medium`, `long` y `full` de cada idioma (incluyendo declinaciones como `\"2026ko urriaren 31\"` en euskera o `\"31 d'octubre de 2026\"` en catalán).\n3. **Formateo numérico con agrupación de miles y redondeo decimal *half-away-from-zero* (`format int`, `format decimal`)**: aplica separadores de miles (`.`, `,`, espacio o NBSP `\\u00a0`) y separador decimal según el locale, con descomposición binaria IEEE-754 de 53 pasos sin `libc`.\n4. **Autónimos nativos (`language name`) y normalización BCP-47 (`normalize locale`)**: convierte etiquetas como `\"es_ES.UTF-8\"` o `\"pt-BR\"` a su código base (`\"es\"`, `\"pt\"`) con fallback determinista a `\"en\"` y devuelve el autónimo nativo (`\"Español\"`, `\"Català\"`, `\"Galego\"`, `\"Euskara\"`, `\"English\"`, `\"Português\"`, `\"Svenska\"`, `\"Italiano\"`, etc.).\n\n---\n\n## 34.2. Explorando `locale` a fondo: Ejemplos paso a paso de cada funcionalidad\n\n### 34.3.1. Ejemplo 1: Reglas de plurales CLDR (modo `.po` de 2 formas y modo estricto CLDR 46 con `\"many\"`)\n\n```ridgun\nfn :: test locale plural rules => ()\n      test locale plural rules =\n        assert str eq (plural category \"es\" 1) \"one\" \"AC2: es 1 -> one\"\n        assert str eq (plural category \"es\" 0) \"other\" \"AC2: es 0 -> other\"\n        assert str eq (plural category \"es\" 5) \"other\" \"AC2: es 5 -> other\"\n        assert str eq (plural category \"es\" 1000000) \"other\" \"AC2: es 1000000 default .po -> other\"\n        assert str eq (plural category \"eu\" 1) \"one\" \"AC2: eu 1 -> one\"\n        assert str eq (plural category \"eu\" 2) \"other\" \"AC2: eu 2 -> other\"\n        assert str eq (plural category \"sv\" 1) \"one\" \"AC2: sv 1 -> one\"\n        assert str eq (plural category \"sv\" 2) \"other\" \"AC2: sv 2 -> other\"\n        assert str eq (plural category \"ca\" 1) \"one\" \"AC2: ca 1 -> one\"\n        assert str eq (plural category \"gl\" 1) \"one\" \"AC2: gl 1 -> one\"\n        assert str eq (plural category \"pt\" 1) \"one\" \"AC2: pt 1 -> one\"\n        assert str eq (plural category \"en\" 1) \"one\" \"AC2: en 1 -> one\"\n        assert str eq (plural category \"it\" 1) \"one\" \"AC2: it 1 -> one\"\n        assert str eq (plural category \"it\" 5) \"other\" \"AC2: it 5 -> other\"\n        assert str eq (plural category \"zz\" 1) \"one\" \"AC2: unknown 1 -> one\"\n        assert str eq (plural category \"zz\" 3) \"other\" \"AC2: unknown 3 -> other\"\n\n        assert str eq (loc join strs (plural categories \"es\")) \"one,other\" \"AC2: default plural categories es\"\n        assert str eq (loc join strs (plural categories \"eu\")) \"one,other\" \"AC2: default plural categories eu\"\n        assert str eq (loc join strs (plural categories \"it\")) \"one,other\" \"AC2: default plural categories it\"\n\n        assert int equals (plural index \"es\" 1) 0 \"AC2: plural index 1 -> 0\"\n        assert int equals (plural index \"es\" 5) 1 \"AC2: plural index 5 -> 1\"\n        assert int equals (plural index \"it\" 1) 0 \"AC2: plural index it 1 -> 0\"\n        assert int equals (plural index \"it\" 5) 1 \"AC2: plural index it 5 -> 1\"\n\n        assert str eq (plural category cldr \"es\" 1000000) \"many\" \"AC2: strict CLDR es 1000000 -> many\"\n        assert str eq (plural category cldr \"ca\" 2000000) \"many\" \"AC2: strict CLDR ca 2000000 -> many\"\n        assert str eq (plural category cldr \"pt\" 1000000) \"many\" \"AC2: strict CLDR pt 1000000 -> many\"\n        assert str eq (plural category cldr \"it\" 1) \"one\" \"AC2: strict CLDR it 1 -> one\"\n        assert str eq (plural category cldr \"it\" 1000000) \"many\" \"AC2: strict CLDR it 1000000 -> many\"\n        assert str eq (plural category cldr \"it\" 5) \"other\" \"AC2: strict CLDR it 5 -> other\"\n        assert str eq (plural category cldr \"es\" 0) \"other\" \"AC2: strict CLDR es 0 -> other\"\n        assert str eq (plural category cldr \"eu\" 1000000) \"other\" \"AC2: strict CLDR eu 1000000 -> other\"\n        assert str eq (loc join strs (plural categories cldr \"es\")) \"one,many,other\" \"AC2: strict CLDR categories es\"\n        assert str eq (loc join strs (plural categories cldr \"it\")) \"one,many,other\" \"AC2: strict CLDR categories it\"\n        assert str eq (loc join strs (plural categories cldr \"sv\")) \"one,other\" \"AC2: strict CLDR categories sv\"\n        assert int equals (plural index cldr \"it\" 1) 0 \"AC2: plural index cldr it 1 -> 0 (one)\"\n        assert int equals (plural index cldr \"it\" 1000000) 1 \"AC2: plural index cldr it 1000000 -> 1 (many)\"\n        assert int equals (plural index cldr \"it\" 5) 2 \"AC2: plural index cldr it 5 -> 2 (other)\"\n        ()\n```\n\n### Ejemplo 3: Formateo de enteros y decimales con agrupación de miles por locale\n\n```ridgun\nfn :: test locale numbers => ()\n      test locale numbers =\n        nbsp = (char from code 194) + (char from code 160)\n        assert str eq (format int \"es\" 1234567) \"1.234.567\" \"AC4: format int es 1234567\"\n        assert str eq (format int \"ca\" 1234567) \"1.234.567\" \"AC4: format int ca 1234567\"\n        assert str eq (format int \"eu\" 1234567) \"1.234.567\" \"AC4: format int eu 1234567\"\n        assert str eq (format int \"gl\" 1234567) \"1.234.567\" \"AC4: format int gl 1234567\"\n        assert str eq (format int \"pt\" 1234567) \"1.234.567\" \"AC4: format int pt 1234567\"\n        assert str eq (format int \"sv\" 1234567) (\"1\" + nbsp + \"234\" + nbsp + \"567\") \"AC4: format int sv 1234567 with NBSP\"\n        assert str eq (format int \"en\" 1234567) \"1,234,567\" \"AC4: format int en 1234567\"\n        assert str eq (format int \"it\" 1234567) \"1.234.567\" \"AC4: format int it 1234567\"\n        assert str eq (format int \"es\" (-1234567)) \"-1.234.567\" \"AC4: format int es negative\"\n        assert str eq (format int \"es\" 42) \"42\" \"AC4: format int es small\"\n        assert str eq (format int \"es\" 0) \"0\" \"AC4: format int es zero\"\n\n        assert str eq (format decimal \"es\" 1234567.89 2) \"1.234.567,89\" \"AC4: format decimal es\"\n        assert str eq (format decimal \"sv\" 1234.5 2) (\"1\" + nbsp + \"234,50\") \"AC4: format decimal sv\"\n        assert str eq (format decimal \"en\" 1234.5 2) \"1,234.50\" \"AC4: format decimal en\"\n        assert str eq (format decimal \"it\" 1234.5 2) \"1.234,50\" \"AC4: format decimal it\"\n        assert str eq (format decimal \"es\" (-19.99) 2) \"-19,99\" \"AC4: format decimal negative\"\n        ()\n```\n\n### 34.3.4. Ejemplo 4: Autónimos de idiomas (`language name`) y normalización BCP-47 / POSIX\n\n```ridgun\nfn :: test locale autonyms normalization and registry => ()\n      test locale autonyms normalization and registry =\n        assert str eq (loc join strs (supported locales)) \"es,ca,eu,gl,pt,sv,en,it\" \"AC1: supported locales order\"\n        assert str eq (language name \"es\") \"Español\" \"AC1: language name es\"\n        assert str eq (language name \"ca\") \"Català\" \"AC1: language name ca\"\n        assert str eq (language name \"eu\") \"Euskara\" \"AC1: language name eu\"\n        assert str eq (language name \"gl\") \"Galego\" \"AC1: language name gl\"\n        assert str eq (language name \"pt\") \"Português\" \"AC1: language name pt\"\n        assert str eq (language name \"sv\") \"Svenska\" \"AC1: language name sv\"\n        assert str eq (language name \"en\") \"English\" \"AC1: language name en\"\n        assert str eq (language name \"it\") \"Italiano\" \"AC1: language name it\"\n        assert str eq (language name \"unknown\") \"English\" \"AC1: unknown locale falls back to English\"\n        assert str eq (language name \"root\") \"English\" \"AC1: root locale falls back to English\"\n        assert str eq (normalize locale \"es-ES\") \"es\" \"AC1: normalize locale es-ES\"\n        assert str eq (normalize locale \"CA_ES.UTF-8\") \"ca\" \"AC1: normalize locale CA_ES.UTF-8\"\n        assert str eq (normalize locale \"pt-BR\") \"pt\" \"AC1: normalize locale pt-BR\"\n        assert str eq (normalize locale \"it_IT.UTF-8\") \"it\" \"AC1: normalize locale it_IT.UTF-8\"\n        assert str eq (normalize locale \"xx-YY\") \"en\" \"AC1: normalize unknown locale to en\"\n\n        fr_spec = LocaleSpec \"fr\" \"Français\" \"one_zero_one\" Garantías algorítmicas, memoria `RMM1`/`RMM2` y cierre del libro\n\n- **Garantía algorítmica y de seguridad**: Funciones 100 % puras y sin estado global mutable (`TZ` / `LC_ALL`), calendario civil UTC en $O(1)$ con validación de años bisiestos y fallback determinista a `\"en\"` ante etiquetas desconocidas.\n- **Complejidad de pila $O(1)$ con TCO**: Todos los recorridos de sustitución y agrupación en `src/main/ridgun/lib/locale.ridgun` son recursivos de cola.\n- **Verificación continua**: Probada exhaustivamente con `src/test/ridgun/test locale.ridgun`.\n\n¡Has completado el recorrido exhaustivo por las **38 libs estándar de `ridgun-libs`**!\n\n---\n\nEn el **Capítulo 35** pasaremos a explorar en profundidad la lib **`hash`** (La lib `hash` — Hashing con Clave SipHash-1-3 para Tablas Hash).\n"}, {"num": "34", "slug": "35-lib-hash-hashing-siphash-con-clave", "file": "35-lib-hash-hashing-siphash-con-clave.md", "title": "Capítulo 35: La lib `hash` — Hashing con Clave SipHash-1-3 para Tablas Hash", "short_title": "La lib `hash` — Hashing con Clave SipHash-1-3 para Tablas Hash", "markdown": "# Capítulo 35: La lib `hash` — Hashing con Clave SipHash-1-3 para Tablas Hash\n\n## 35.1. ¿Por qué existe la lib `hash`? (El problema real y la filosofía Ridgun)\n\n> *«¿Por qué necesito una lib `hash` escrita desde cero en Ridgun puro en lugar de enlazar una librería de C de toda la vida?»*\n\nEsa es la primera pregunta que se hace cualquier ingeniero de sistemas al llegar a `hash`. Y la respuesta resume toda la filosofía de `ridgun-libs`:\n\nSeamos sinceros: cuando la función hash de una tabla hash es pública, quien controla las claves puede enviar miles que caen en la misma ranura, y una sola petición cuesta entonces lo que debería costar un millón (hash flooding).\n\nLa lib **`hash`** implementa **SipHash-1-3** (Aumasson & Bernstein) con una clave de 128 bits y un resultado de 64 bits. `siphash13` calcula el hash de una cadena completa; las operaciones nativas del compilador `siphash13 range` y `siphash13 range low` (ridgunc 1.0.44) calculan el hash de un rango de bytes en unas decenas de nanosegundos; `siphash13 reference` es el mismo hash escrito en Ridgun llano, para leerlo y para probar contra él; y `siphash new key` obtiene del sistema una clave aleatoria de 16 bytes.\n\nEn un ecosistema tradicional, resolver las tareas del dominio **`HASH`** implica arrastrar dependencias externas en C, lidiar con punteros crudos, conversiones opacas de tipos, excepciones no verificadas o pausas impredecibles del recolector de basura. En Ridgun, la lib **`hash`** (`src/main/ridgun/lib/hash.ridgun`) aborda el problema con cuatro principios innegociables:\n\n1. **Declara `import hash` (o `import hash as alias`) al inicio del archivo**: cada lib define su espacio de nombres `module :: hash` y en modo `--strict` las funciones multi-palabra se invocan siempre con espacios naturales.\n2. **Encadena tus tuberías de izquierda a derecha con `->`**: escribe `entrada paso uno -> paso dos -> resultado`, usa máscaras `(+ _ _ +)` para desestructurar secuencias y omite `_ =` en sentencias secuenciales (o descarta con `-> ()`).\n3. **Recursión de cola con TCO (*Tail-Call Optimization*)**: todos los recorridos internos de `hash` se compilan a bucles nativos en $O(1)$ espacio de pila.\n4. **Memoria determinista (`RMM1` / `RMM2`)**: cada estructura intermedia se libera en el instante exacto en que termina su última lectura, sin *Garbage Collector*.\n\n---\n\n## 35.2. Artefactos nativos, importación y catálogo completo de la API de `hash`\n\nEn `ridgun-libs`, **`hash`** es una **lib** de primera clase ubicada en `src/main/ridgun/lib/hash.ridgun` (dominio `HASH`). Bajo el capó: cómo está construida `hash` en Ridgun puro (`src/main/ridgun/lib/hash.ridgun`)\n\nUna de las mayores ventajas de `ridgun-libs` es que **no hay cajas negras en C**. Puedes abrir `src/main/ridgun/lib/hash.ridgun` y leer exactamente cómo está implementada cada operación usando *pattern matching*, árboles de guardas `|` / `|.` y recursión de cola (TCO). Veamos las piezas clave de su implementación real:\n\n### 35.4.1. Implementación interna: SipRound on 32-Bit Halves: One Message Word per Turn\n\nFíjate en cómo `hash.ridgun` estructura las firmas `fn :: ... => ...` primero y resuelve cada caso mediante ecuaciones alineadas y llamadas de cola:\n\n```ridgun\n-- The byte at `i` as 0..255.\nfn :: hs byte String Int => Int\n      hs byte s i =  (str char at s i) and 255\n\n-- The byte at `i`, or 0 at or after `to`.\nfn :: hs tail String Int Int => Int\n      hs tail s i to =\n        | i >= to   = 0\n        | otherwise = (str char at s i) and 255\n\nfn :: hs pick Int Int Int => Int\n      hs pick want hi lo =\n        | want == 0 = lo\n        | otherwise = (hi shl 32) or lo\n\n-- Little-endian 32-bit word of the key at `off`.\nfn :: hs key word String Int => Int\n      hs key word k off =  (hs byte k off) or ((hs byte k (off + 1)) shl 8) or ((hs byte k (off + 2)) shl 16) or ((hs byte k (off + 3)) shl 24)\n\n-- One message word per turn: v3 ^= m, 1 round(s), v0 ^= m. The 8 state values are the halves of v0..v3.\nfn :: siphash13 loop String Int Int Int Int Int Int Int Int Int Int Int Int Int => Int\n      siphash13 loop s off full to n want a0 b0 a1 b1 a2 b2 a3 b3 =\n        | off >= full = siphash13 last s off to n want a0 b0 a1 b1 a2 b2 a3 b3\n        | otherwise   =\n          t1 = (hs byte s off) or ((hs byte s (off + 1)) shl 8) or ((hs byte s (off + 2)) shl 16) or ((hs byte s (off + 3)) shl 24)\n          t2 = (hs byte s (off + 4)) or ((hs byte s (off + 5)) shl 8) or ((hs byte s (off + 6)) shl 16) or ((hs byte s (off + 7)) shl 24)\n          t3 = a3 xor t2\n          t4 = b3 xor t1\n          t5 = b0 + b1\n          t6 = ((a0 + a1) + (t5 shr 32)) and 0xFFFFFFFF\n          t7 = t5 and 0xFFFFFFFF\n          t8 = ((a1 shl 13) or (b1 shr 19)) and 0xFFFFFFFF\n          t9 = ((b1 shl 13) or (a1 shr 19)) and 0xFFFFFFFF\n          t10 = t8 xor t6\n          t11 = t9 xor t7\n          t12 = b2 + t4\n          t13 = ((a2 + t3) + (t12 shr 32)) and 0xFFFFFFFF\n          t14 = t12 and 0xFFFFFFFF\n          t15 = ((t3 shl 16) or (t4 shr 16)) and 0xFFFFFFFF\n          t16 = ((t4 shl 16) or (t3 shr 16)) and 0xFFFFFFFF\n          t17 = t15 xor t13\n          t18 = t16 xor t14\n          t19 = t6 + t18\n          t20 = ((t7 + t17) + (t19 shr 32)) and 0xFFFFFFFF\n          t21 = t19 and 0xFFFFFFFF\n          t22 = ((t17 shl 21) or (t18 shr 11)) and 0xFFFFFFFF\n          t23 = ((t18 shl 21) or (t17 shr 11)) and 0xFFFFFFFF\n          t24 = t22 xor t20\n          t25 = t23 xor t21\n          t26 = t14 + t11\n          t27 = ((t13 + t10) + (t26 shr 32)) and 0xFFFFFFFF\n          t28 = t26 and 0xFFFFFFFF\n          t29 = ((t10 shl 17) or (t11 shr 15)) and 0xFFFFFFFF\n          t30 = ((t11 shl 17) or (t10 shr 15)) and 0xFFFFFFFF\n          t31 = t29 xor t27\n          t32 = t30 xor t28\n          t33 = t20 xor t2\n          t34 = t21 xor t1\n          siphash13 loop s (off + 8) full to n want t33 t34 t31 t32 t28 t27 t24 t25\n```\n\n### 35.4.2. Implementación interna: Public API: `siphash13`, the Plain-Ridgun Reference, and Random Keys\n\nFíjate en cómo `hash.ridgun` estructura las firmas `fn :: ... => ...` primero y resuelve cada caso mediante ecuaciones alineadas y llamadas de cola:\n\n```ridgun\n-- v0..v3 from the key (k0 = bytes 0-7, k1 = bytes 8-15, little-endian) and the constants \"somepseudorandomlygeneratedbytes\".\nfn :: siphash13 start String String Int Int Int => Int\n      siphash13 start key s from to want =\n        k0l = hs key word key 0\n        k0h = hs key word key 4\n        k1l = hs key word key 8\n        k1h = hs key word key 12\n        n   = to - from\n        siphash13 loop s from (from + ((n shr 3) shl 3)) to n want (k0h xor 0x736f6d65) (k0l xor 0x70736575) (k1h xor 0x646f7261) (k1l xor 0x6e646f6d) (k0h xor 0x6c796765) (k0l xor 0x6e657261) (k1h xor 0x74656462) (k1l xor 0x79746573)\n\n-- `siphash13 range key data from to` (64 bits) and `siphash13 range low key data from to` (the low 32 bits)\n-- are operations of the compiler since ridgunc 1.0.44: native, some tens of ns for a short key. They take\n-- a 16-byte key and the bytes `from` (included) to `to` (excluded) of `data`; a key of another length or a\n-- range outside `data` gives 0. This lib does not define them, so that the native ones are used.\n\n-- SipHash-1-3 of the whole of `data`.\nfn :: siphash13 String String => Int\n      siphash13 key data =  siphash13 range key data 0 (str len data)\n\n-- The same hash written in plain Ridgun (about 2 µs for a 25-byte key): the definition the native operation\n-- is tested against, and the one to read. `want` 0 gives the low 32 bits, anything else the 64 bits.\nfn :: siphash13 reference String String Int Int Int => Int\n      siphash13 reference key data from to want =\n        | (str len key) != 16 or from < 0 or to < from or to > (str len data) = 0\n        | otherwise = siphash13 start key data from to want\n\n-- A new random 16-byte key (from the system random source). \"\" when it cannot be read.\nfn :: siphash new key => String\n      siphash new key =  hs key of (sys random bytes 16)\n\nfn :: hs key of (Int String) => String\n      hs key of (rc, k) =\n        | rc == 0 and (str len k) == 16 = k\n        | otherwise                     = \"\"\n```\n\n---\n\n## 35.5. Garantías algorítmicas, memoria `RMM1`/`RMM2` y las 5 Reglas de Oro de `hash`\n\n- **Garantía algorítmica y de seguridad**: Una clave de otra longitud, o un rango fuera de los datos, da `0` en lugar de leer fuera de los límites, y la operación nativa devuelve los mismos 64 bits que la referencia en Ridgun llano para todas las longitudes y desplazamientos probados.\n- **Complejidad de pila $O(1)$ con TCO**: Todos los bucles recursivos en `src/main/ridgun/lib/hash.ridgun` están en posición de cola, por lo que `ridgunc` los compila a saltos nativos sin crecimiento de pila.\n- **Memoria determinista (`RMM1`/`RMM2`)**: Cero pausas de recolector de basura; En Ridgun, la lib **`hashmap`** (`src/main/ridgun/lib/hashmap.ridgun`) aborda el problema con cuatro principios innegociables:\n\n1. **Declara `import hashmap` (o `import hashmap as alias`) al inicio del archivo**: cada lib define su espacio de nombres `module :: hashmap` y en modo `--strict` las funciones multi-palabra se invocan siempre con espacios naturales.\n2. **Encadena tus tuberías de izquierda a derecha con `->`**: escribe `entrada paso uno -> paso dos -> resultado`, usa máscaras `(+ _ _ +)` para desestructurar secuencias y omite `_ =` en sentencias secuenciales (o descarta con `-> ()`).\n3. **Recursión de cola con TCO (*Tail-Call Optimization*)**: todos los recorridos internos de `hashmap` se compilan a bucles nativos en $O(1)$ espacio de pila.\n4. **Memoria determinista (`RMM1` / `RMM2`)**: cada estructura intermedia se libera en el instante exacto en que termina su última lectura, sin *Garbage Collector*.\n\n---\n\n## 36.2. Artefactos nativos, importación y catálogo completo de la API de `hashmap`\n\nEn `ridgun-libs`, **`hashmap`** es una **lib** de primera clase ubicada en `src/main/ridgun/lib/hashmap.ridgun` (dominio `HASHMAP`). Al compilar con `stable bundle`, se empaqueta en un artefacto nativo:\n\n| Artefacto | Ruta | Propósito |\n|---|---|---|\n| **Bundle Ridgun** | `target/bundles/hashmap.ridgunlib` | Distribución e importación directa con `import hashmap` |\n\n> Cada lib declara su propio espacio de nombres con `module :: hashmap`: basta con escribir `import hashmap` (o `import hashmap as alias`) en el encabezado y llamar a sus funciones con espacios naturales (`mi funcion x`) y tuberías `->` (`x mi funcion -> resultado`).\n\n### 36.2.1. Explorando `hashmap` a fondo: Ejemplos paso a paso de cada funcionalidad\n\nNo basta con ver la tabla de firmas: vamos a explorar **cada una de las funcionalidades** de la lib `hashmap` mediante ejemplos progresivos y ejecutables en Ridgun. Empezaremos por las dos recetas tabulares de uso cotidiano y después recorreremos en detalle todos los escenarios funcionales, transformaciones y casos límite verificados en `src/test/ridgun/test hashmap.ridgun`.\n\n### 36.3.1. Ejemplo 1: Flujo principal en estilo tabular con `hashmap`\n\nObserva cómo en Ridgun los signos `=` y los pasos de transformación con `hashmap` quedan alineados como una tabla limpia, sin variables mutables innecesarias ni efectos laterales ocultos:\n\n```ridgun\nimport hashmap\n\nfn :: contar visitas [String]     (HashMap Int) => HashMap Int\n      contar visitas []           m             =  m\n      contar visitas (ruta:resto) m             =  contar visitas resto (hashmap add m ruta 1)\n```\n\n### 36.3.2. Ejemplo 2: Composición segura y manejo de casos de borde\n\nToda función de la lib `hashmap` está diseñada para componerse con guardas booleanas `|` y con el resto de las 38 libs de `ridgun-libs`:\n\n```ridgun\nimport hashmap\n\nfn :: visitas de (HashMap Int) String => Int\n      visitas de m ruta =\n        | hashmap has m ruta = hashmap get m ruta 0\n        | otherwise          = 0\n```\n\n### 36.3.3. Ejemplo 3: El mapa vacío, `hashmap put`, reemplazo, `hashmap get` con valor por defecto y `hashmap pairs`\n\nEn este ejemplo práctico exploramos de forma exhaustiva cómo se comporta `hashmap` en este bloque funcional, incluyendo entradas estándar, combinaciones de parámetros y valores frontera:\n\n```ridgun\nfn :: test hashmap basics => ()\n      test hashmap basics =\n        e = hashmap empty\n        hashmap get e \"a\" 7 -> assert int equals 7 \"AC1: get on empty gives the default\"\n        hashmap has e \"a\" -> assert false \"AC1: has on empty\"\n        hashmap size e -> assert int equals 0 \"AC1: size of empty\"\n        hashmap pairs e -> assert eq []\n\n        m = hashmap put (hashmap put (hashmap put hashmap empty \"b\" 2) \"a\" 1) \"c\" 3\n        m2 = hashmap put m \"a\" 10\n        hashmap get m2 \"a\" 0 -> assert int equals 10 \"AC1: put replaces the value\"\n        hashmap get m2 \"b\" 0 -> assert int equals 2 \"AC1: get b\"\n        hashmap get m2 \"zz\" (0 - 1) -> assert int equals (0 - 1) \"AC1: missing key gives the default\"\n        hashmap has m2 \"c\" -> assert true \"AC1: has c\"\n        hashmap has m2 \"zz\" -> assert false \"AC1: has missing\"\n        hashmap size m2 -> assert int equals 3 \"AC1: replacing does not add a key\"\n        hashmap pairs m2 -> assert eq [(\"b\", 2), (\"a\", 10), (\"c\", 3)]\n        ()\n```\n\n### 36.3.4. Ejemplo 4: Contadores con `hashmap add`: sumas, claves ausentes y llegada a cero\n\nEn este ejemplo práctico exploramos de forma exhaustiva cómo se comporta `hashmap` en este bloque funcional, incluyendo entradas estándar, combinaciones de parámetros y valores frontera:\n\n```ridgun\nfn :: test hashmap add => ()\n      test hashmap add =\n        m = hashmap add (hashmap add (hashmap add hashmap empty \"x\" 2) \"y\" 5) \"x\" 3\n        hashmap get m \"x\" 0 -> assert int equals 5 \"AC2: add sums\"\n        hashmap get m \"y\" 0 -> assert int equals 5 \"AC2: a missing key starts at 0\"\n        m2 = hashmap add m \"y\" (0 - 5)\n        hashmap get m2 \"y\" 99 -> assert int equals 0 \"AC2: add can reach 0 and the key stays\"\n        hashmap has m2 \"y\" -> assert true \"AC2: has after reaching 0\"\n        hashmap pairs m2 -> assert eq [(\"x\", 5), (\"y\", 0)]\n        ()\n```\n\n### 36.3.5. Ejemplo 5: Claves inusuales: la cadena vacía, bytes por encima de 127 y claves de 10 KB que difieren en el último byte\n\nEn este ejemplo práctico exploramos de forma exhaustiva cómo se comporta `hashmap` en este bloque funcional, incluyendo entradas estándar, combinaciones de parámetros y valores frontera:\n\n```ridgun\nfn :: test hashmap unusual keys => ()\n      test hashmap unusual keys =\n        hi = (char from code 200) + (char from code 255)\n        la = kb10 \"a\"\n        lb = kb10 \"b\"\n        m = hashmap put (hashmap put (hashmap put (hashmap put hashmap empty \"\" 1) hi 2) la 3) lb 4\n        hashmap get m \"\" 0 -> assert int equals 1 \"AC3: empty key\"\n        hashmap get m hi 0 -> assert int equals 2 \"AC3: bytes >= 128\"\n        hashmap get m la 0 -> assert int equals 3 \"AC3: 10 KB key\"\n        hashmap get m lb 0 -> assert int equals 4 \"AC3: 10 KB key differing in the last byte\"\n        hashmap has m (kb10 \"c\") -> assert false \"AC3: another 10 KB key is missing\"\n        hashmap has m (char from code 200) -> assert false \"AC3: prefix of a key is missing\"\n        hashmap size m -> assert int equals 4 \"AC3: four keys\"\n        ()\n```\n\n### 36.3.6. Ejemplo 6: Valores de tipo registro: un `HashMap` de registros definidos por el usuario\n\nEn este ejemplo práctico exploramos de forma exhaustiva cómo se comporta `hashmap` en este bloque funcional, incluyendo entradas estándar, combinaciones de parámetros y valores frontera:\n\n```ridgun\nfn :: test hashmap record values => ()\n      test hashmap record values =\n        m = hashmap put (hashmap put (hashmap put hashmap empty \"/a\" (Visit \"/a\" 3)) \"/b\" (Visit \"/b\" 7)) \"/a\" (Visit \"/a\" 4)\n        hashmap get m \"/a\" (Visit \"\" 0) -> assert eq (Visit \"/a\" 4)\n        hashmap get m \"/b\" (Visit \"\" 0) -> assert eq (Visit \"/b\" 7)\n        hashmap get m \"/c\" (Visit \"\" 0) -> assert eq (Visit \"\" 0)\n        hits (hashmap get m \"/a\" (Visit \"\" 0)) -> assert int equals 4 \"AC4: record field\"\n        ()\n```\n\n### 36.3.7. Ejemplo 7: Crecimiento: 20 000 claves, todas las claves encontradas y orden de inserción conservado\n\nEn este ejemplo práctico exploramos de forma exhaustiva cómo se comporta `hashmap` en este bloque funcional, incluyendo entradas estándar, combinaciones de parámetros y valores frontera:\n\n```ridgun\nfn :: test hashmap growth => ()\n      test hashmap growth =\n        n = 20000\n        m = put many hashmap empty 0 n\n        hashmap size m -> assert int equals n \"AC1: 20000 keys after growing\"\n        all found m 0 n -> assert true \"AC1: every key found after growing\"\n        ps = hashmap pairs m\n        sum values ps 0 -> assert int equals (n * (n - 1) / 2) \"AC1: pairs hold every value\"\n        first keys ps 3 [] -> assert eq [\"key 0\", \"key 1\", \"key 2\"]\n        fill 1 + count [] + str len seed -> assert int equals 7 \"Program functions named like fields still work\"\n        ()\n```\n\n---\n\n## 36.4. Bajo el capó: cómo está construida `hashmap` en Ridgun puro (`src/main/ridgun/lib/hashmap.ridgun`)\n\nUna de las mayores ventajas de `ridgun-libs` es que **no hay cajas negras en C**. Puedes abrir `src/main/ridgun/lib/hashmap.ridgun` y leer exactamente cómo está implementada cada operación usando *pattern matching*, árboles de guardas `|` / `|.` y recursión de cola (TCO). Veamos las piezas clave de su implementación real:\n\n### 36.4.1. Implementación interna: Hash\n\nFíjate en cómo `hashmap.ridgun` estructura las firmas `fn :: ... => ...` primero y resuelve cada caso mediante ecuaciones alineadas y llamadas de cola:\n\n```ridgun\n-- 31 bits of SipHash-1-3 of the key, with the map's 16-byte seed as the hash key (the compiler's native\n-- `siphash13 range low`, ridgunc 1.0.44), plus 1 so a used slot is never 0.\n-- Keys are always compared when the hashes match.\n-- The per-map random seed stops chosen keys from colliding on purpose.\nfn :: hm hash String String => Int\n      hm hash seed key =  ((siphash13 range low seed key 0 (str len key)) % 2147483648) + 1\n\n-- Exactly 16 bytes: SipHash takes a 128-bit key.\nfn :: hm seed16 String => String\n      hm seed16 s =\n        | (str len s) == 16 = s\n        | otherwise         = str slice (s + \"ridgun-hashmap-0\") 0 16\n\nfn :: hm read seed Int => String\n      hm read seed fd =\n        | fd < 0    = hm seed16 (int to str (sys time ms))\n        | otherwise =\n          s = sys read fd fd 16\n          sys close fd -> ()\n          hm seed16 s\n\nfn :: hm new seed => String\n      hm new seed = hm read seed (sys open mode \"/dev/urandom\" \"r\")\n```\n\n### 36.4.2. Implementación interna: Slots\n\nFíjate en cómo `hashmap.ridgun` estructura las firmas `fn :: ... => ...` primero y resuelve cada caso mediante ecuaciones alineadas y llamadas de cola:\n\n```ridgun\nfn :: hm slot hash Int => Int\n      hm slot hash s = s / 2147483648\n\n-- Slot of key k with hash h: the slot that holds it, or the free slot where it goes.\n-- Hot path: the slot is decoded inline (each call costs about 20 ns).\nfn :: hm probe Tensor[Int * n] Tensor[String * m] Int String Int Int => Int\n      hm probe slots keys cap k h i =\n        | slots_(i) == 0                          = i\n        | slots_(i) / 2147483648 != h             = hm probe slots keys cap k h ((i + 1) % cap)\n        | keys_(slots_(i) % 2147483648) == k      = i\n        | otherwise                               = hm probe slots keys cap k h ((i + 1) % cap)\n\n-- First free slot from i; for rehashing, where every key is known to be new.\nfn :: hm free Tensor[Int * n] Int Int => Int\n      hm free slots cap i =\n        | slots_(i) == 0 = i\n        | otherwise      = hm free slots cap ((i + 1) % cap)\n```\n\n### 36.4.3. Implementación interna: Table\n\nFíjate en cómo `hashmap.ridgun` estructura las firmas `fn :: ... => ...` primero y resuelve cada caso mediante ecuaciones alineadas y llamadas de cola:\n\n```ridgun\nfn :: hashmap empty => HashMap V\n      hashmap empty = HashMap [] [] (Tensor[Int * 16]) (Tensor[String * 8]) 16 8 (Tensor[Int * 1]) (hm new seed)\n\nfn :: hm size (HashMap V) => Int\n      hm size m = (count m)_(0)\n\nfn :: hm bump Tensor[Int * k] => ()\n      hm bump t =\n        t_(0) = t_(0) + 1\n\nfn :: hm vt [Tensor[V * n]] => Tensor[V * n]\n      hm vt (t:_) = t\n\n-- Copies every used slot to the new table, by its stored hash. Int only.\nfn :: hm rehash Tensor[Int * n] Tensor[Int * m] Int Int Int => ()\n      hm rehash old new i ocap ncap =\n        | i >= ocap     = ()\n        | old_(i) == 0  = hm rehash old new (i + 1) ocap ncap\n        | otherwise     =\n          s = old_(i)\n          new_(hm free new ncap ((hm slot hash s) % ncap)) = s\n          hm rehash old new (i + 1) ocap ncap\n\nfn :: hm grow slots (HashMap V) => HashMap V\n      hm grow slots m =\n        ncap = 2 * (cap m)\n        ns   = Tensor[Int * ncap]\n        hm rehash (slots m) ns 0 (cap m) ncap\n        m with slots = ns, cap = ncap\n\nfn :: hm copy Tensor[String * n] Tensor[V * n] Tensor[String * m] Tensor[V * m] Int Int => ()\n      hm copy ok ov nk nv i n =\n        | i >= n    = ()\n        | otherwise =\n          nk_(i) = ok_(i)\n          nv_(i) = ov_(i)\n          hm copy ok ov nk nv (i + 1) n\n\nfn :: hm grow dense (HashMap V) [V] => HashMap V\n      hm grow dense m (d:_) =\n        nr = 2 * (room m)\n        nk = Tensor[String * nr]\n        nv = Tensor[V * nr] with d\n        hm copy (keys m) (hm vt (vals m)) nk nv 0 (hm size m)\n        m with keys = nk, vals = [nv], room = nr\n\n-- Keeps the slot table at most half full and room for one more key.\nfn :: hm make room (HashMap V) => HashMap V\n      hm make room m = hm room dense (hm room slots m)\n\nfn :: hm room slots (HashMap V) => HashMap V\n      hm room slots m =\n        | 2 * ((hm size m) + 1) > cap m = hm grow slots m\n        | otherwise                      = m\n\nfn :: hm room dense (HashMap V) => HashMap V\n      hm room dense m =\n        | (hm size m) + 1 > room m = hm grow dense m (fill m)\n        | otherwise                  = m\n\n-- The first insert supplies the fill value for the value tensor.\nfn :: hm ensure vals (HashMap V) V => HashMap V\n      hm ensure vals m v = m with fill = [v], vals = [Tensor[V * (room m)] with v]\n\n-- Puts a new key at the next position and points slot i at it.\nfn :: hm insert Tensor[V * n] Tensor[Int * c] Tensor[String * r] Tensor[Int * k] Int Int String V => ()\n      hm insert vt st kt cnt i h k v =\n        pos = cnt_(0)\n        kt_(pos) = k\n        vt_(pos) = v\n        st_(i) = h * 2147483648 + pos\n        cnt_(0) = pos + 1\n\n-- The hot paths take the record apart once in the clause: each field accessor\n-- is a call of about 40 ns.\n\nfn :: hm put go (HashMap V) (HashMap V) String V => HashMap V\n      hm put go m (HashMap []   _      _  _  _   _    _   _   ) k v = hashmap put (hm ensure vals m v) k v\n      hm put go m (HashMap _ (vt:_) st kt cap room cnt seed) k v =\n        | 2 * (cnt_(0) + 1) > cap or cnt_(0) + 1 > room = hashmap put (hm make room m) k v\n        | otherwise = hm put at m vt st kt cnt k v (hm hash seed k) cap\n\nfn :: hm put at (HashMap V) Tensor[V * n] Tensor[Int * c] Tensor[String * r] Tensor[Int * k] String V Int Int => HashMap V\n      hm put at m vt st kt cnt k v h cap = hm put slot m vt st kt cnt k v h (hm probe st kt cap k h (h % cap))\n\nfn :: hm put slot (HashMap V) Tensor[V * n] Tensor[Int * c] Tensor[String * r] Tensor[Int * k] String V Int Int => HashMap V\n      hm put slot m vt st kt cnt k v h i =\n
